rows: Conveyors can create severe trapping and drawing-in hazards at in-running nips.
Transmission parts and trapping points between moving and fixed components require safeguarding.
Fixed or interlocked guards can prevent access to dangerous parts.
Foreseeable operations such as cleaning and clearing blockages must be included in risk assessment.
Cleaning systems should prevent workers being exposed to unguarded moving parts.
Conveyors should normally be isolated before maintenance or intervention.
Workers need training in conveyor hazards, isolation and safe intervention.
Safeguards and interlocks should be maintained and tested.
An emergency stop or warning label does not prove that nip points are adequately guarded.
Conveyor conclusions require layout, guards, interlocks, isolation, task, maintenance, training and observed-use evidence.
Compressed air contains stored energy that can cause serious injury if released uncontrollably.
Systems should be designed and operated to prevent dangerous overpressurisation.
Air receivers, dryers, coolers, pipework and controls should be suitable for the system.
Blockages, overheating, overspeed and control failure should be considered in risk assessment.
Pressure systems require appropriate inspection, maintenance and competent intervention.
Compressed air should not be directed at the body because it can penetrate skin or body openings.
Particles propelled by compressed air can injure eyes and other exposed tissue.
Workers need information and training on system hazards and safe use.
A pressure gauge reading or service sticker does not prove the whole compressed-air system is safe.
System conclusions require design, pressure limits, protective devices, condition, inspection, maintenance and operating evidence.
Compressed or liquefied gas cylinders can present significant toxic, fire or pressure hazards.
Storage location should reflect the substance hazard, inventory and nearby people or plant.
Cylinders should be stored securely and protected from impact.
Pressurised cylinders should normally be stored with valves uppermost.
Incompatible substances should be appropriately separated.
Suitable trolleys or purpose-designed attachments should be used for cylinder movement.
Leak detection, ventilation and emergency arrangements should reflect the stored gases.
Workers should be trained in connection, disconnection, spill and emergency procedures.
A cylinder label or inventory entry does not prove safe storage and handling.
Conclusions require gas identity, quantity, cylinder condition, storage, segregation, movement, ventilation and emergency evidence.
Designers, installers and operators of battery energy-storage systems have health and safety duties.
Battery systems require control of electrical, fire and explosion hazards.
Risk management should cover the full system lifecycle.
Installation and operation should follow relevant electrical safety requirements.
Dangerous-substance risks should be assessed where flammable or reactive materials may be released.
Emergency planning should consider fire and rescue service information needs.
Site design should account for access, separation and protection of workers and the public.
Changes, faults and incidents should trigger review of controls.
A planning approval or battery specification does not prove operational safety.
Site conclusions require chemistry, design, installation, protection, monitoring, maintenance, fire strategy and emergency evidence.
